column4: Oftentimes in Christianity we think about repentance as fundamental only to the beginning of our faith in Jesus. The heart of repentance goes much deeper than turning away from sin unto salvation. Repentance from dead works means living with our hearts turned away from the things that harm us or stunt our growth-and turned toward the things of God.

column4: While hitting rock-bottom is more a myth than a certain precondition to change, God can use sorrow to influence our minds.  God will use sorrow to bring us to repentance. He will convict us of our actions and the state of our lives and hearts to open our eyes to see our complete and total need of Him.
column5: Although hitting rock bottom is more a myth than a guaranteed prerequisite for change, God can use sorrow to affect our minds. God will use sorrow to lead us to repentance. He will convict us about our actions and the state of our lives and hearts to open our eyes so we see our complete and total need for Him.

column4: Godly sorrow, or <u>the experience of sadness or distress that leads to a *metanoia*</u>, is not the same thing worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of sadness or distress, but the world offers no hope, only the relief and promise of death.
column5: Godly sorrow, or <u>the experience of sorrow or distress that leads to *metanoia*</u>, is not the same as worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of sorrow or distress, but the world offers no hope—only relief and the promise of death.

column4: Sorrow is also different from suffering and grief.
column5: Sorrow is also different from suffering and mourning.

column4: Suffering is the endurance of pain-physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual-especially when prolonged or intense.
column5: Suffering is enduring pain—physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual—especially when it is prolonged or severe.

column4: Grief is a multifaceted emotional response to significant personal loss, especially relational or existential.
column5: Mourning is a multi-faceted emotional response to a significant personal loss, especially one related to relationships or existence.

column4: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related ideas. In the human condition we will experience all three, we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring about death and destruction in our lives to teach us.
column5: Sorrow, suffering, and distress are closely interrelated concepts. In the human condition we will experience all three, and we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring death and destruction into our lives to teach us.

column4: The scriptures say every good and perfect gift is from God above (James 1:17). He is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow will cause discomfort, but His discipline is just and loving. Just as a good father would not intentionally break his child’s arm to ‘teach him a lesson’, God will not inflict sickness or disease on His children to teach us.
column5: The Scriptures say that every good and perfect gift is from God above (James 1:17). And He is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow causes discomfort, but His discipline is just and loving. And just as a good father does not deliberately break his son’s arm to teach him a “lesson,” so God does not inflict sickness or disease on His children to teach us.

column4: ### Example of Worldly Sorrow vs Godly Sorrow
column5: ### An Example of Worldly Sorrow versus Godly Sorrow

column4: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and he intentionally hit her, causing her to cry and leaving a red mark.
column5: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick and deliberately hit her, making her cry and leaving a red mark.

column4: Their father hearing the commotion investigated and when he learned what his son did took the stick, broke it in half and tossed it away. He sent his son inside to think about what did and comforted his daughter.
column5: Their father heard the commotion and looked into it, and when he learned what his son had done he took the stick, broke it in two, and threw it away. He brought his son inside to think about what he had done, and he comforted his daughter.

column4: The father coming inside to deal with his son found him crying. Asking him why he was crying his son said, “because you broke my stick”.
column5: When the father came in to address the matter with his son, he found him crying. He asked why he was crying, and the boy said, “Because you broke my stick.”

column4: The father’s reply was, “I’m sad that you are more concerned about your stick than you are about your sister who you hurt” and sent him back to his room for more reflection.
column5: The father replied, “I am sad that you care more about your stick than about your sister whom you hurt,” and sent him back to his room for further reflection.

column4: A few minutes later his son came back out and apologized. He said he was still sad because dad has broken his stick, and because he had hit his sister.
column5: After a few minutes the boy returned and apologized. He said he was still sad because his father had broken his stick, and because he had hit his sister.

column4: **Progress!**
column5: **Progress!**

column4: In this example the boy experienced both worldly sorrow, for his lost stick, and then eventually godly sorrow, for his hurt sister.
column5: In this example, the boy experienced both kinds of sorrow: worldly sorrow over the stick he lost, and finally godly sorrow over his sister whom he hurt.

column4: Godly sorrow and God’s goodness are connected. God is a good father that will let us experience the consequences of our actions but will still stand beside us as we walk through those consequences.
column5: Godly sorrow and the goodness of God are connected. God is a good Father who allows us to experience the consequences of our actions, but He stands by us as we pass through those consequences.

column4: God's unrelenting goodness, to be willing to redeem us and restore us if we come to Him is a positive agent in our path of repentance. His goodness isn’t that we continue in sin, but that despite our sin He makes a way for us to be redeemed and experience His salvation.
column5: God’s unwavering goodness, and His readiness to redeem and restore us if we come to Him, is a positive factor on the path of our repentance. His goodness is not so that we continue in sin; rather, despite our sins He makes a way for us to be redeemed and to experience His salvation.

In the extreme opposite, for some people the mere example of sin and consequence in someone else’s life is enough to cause them to change their thinking.

By complete contrast, for some people, merely seeing an example of sin and its outcome in another person’s life is enough to move them to change their thinking.

column4: Man has great capacity to change; it's wired into our very essence. Humans are very adaptable, we can learn and grow, and find better ways to do things. However, a capacity to change is not the same as a willingness or a persuasion to change.
column5: Human beings have a great capacity for change; it is rooted in the core of our being. Humans are highly adaptable; we can learn, grow, and find better ways of doing things. However, having the capacity to change is not the same as having the willingness or resolve to change.

column4: I do not know why some people get stuck and others are so ready to change, but I can say that the entire process of change is really from God’s grace.
column5: I do not know why some people get stuck while others are very willing to change, but I can say that the entire process of change is by the grace of God.

Galatians 6:1 reminds us that some will be ‘stuck’ in a trespass (sin) and need help to get unstuck! That help comes in the form of mature men and women who help restore us in a spirit of gentleness.

column4: The Holy Spirit is the greatest agent for change mankind can engage with, and this is backed up by both the scriptures and by research. Research by “Lyons et al. (2010) found that up to 82% of clients who experienced a spiritual awakening during substance abuse treatment and recovery were completely abstinent at a 1-year follow-up compared with 55% of non-spiritually awakened clients.” \\[2\\] While man can initiate and mediate change, we can accomplish so much more when we walk with God’s Spirit.

column4: ### David’s Example of Repentance
column5: ### David’s example of repentance

column4: Perhaps no account in the scriptures has a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin found in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to battle, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her, and they have an affair, resulting in Bathsheba's pregnancy.
column5: Perhaps no account in Scripture offers a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin recorded in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going out to war, where he sees Bathsheba as she is bathing. Although he knows she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her and sleeps with her, and Bathsheba conceives.

column4: To cover his actions, David recalls Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child's father. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go to his home with Bethsheba. David then arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front lines where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah's death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to cover up the pregnancy.
column5: To cover up his actions, David summons Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child’s father. But Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go to his house to be with Bathsheba. David then arranges to send Uriah to the front lines where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah’s death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to conceal the pregnancy.

column4: The Lord is displeased with David's actions and sends the prophet Nathan to confront him. When confronted by the prophet, David immediately admitted, "*I have sinned against the Lord*" (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly to God.
column5: What David had done displeased the Lord, so He sent the prophet Nathan to confront him. And when the prophet confronted him, David immediately confessed: “*I have sinned against the Lord*” (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify his actions or make excuses for them. This confession was the first step in his repentance, as he acknowledged his wrongdoing directly before God.

column4: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his complete ownership of his actions. He expresses grief not only for the sin itself but also for how it offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David displayed "*a broken and contrite heart,*" an essential part of true repentance (Psalms 51:17). This sorrow wasn’t superficial; he deeply grieved over the sin he committed and the hurt it caused. This depth of remorse was a sign that he wanted not only forgiveness but a changed heart.
column5: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me*,” show his full ownership of his actions. He expresses not only sorrow for the sin itself but also for his offense against God, saying: “*Against You, You only, have I sinned*.” David displayed “*a broken and contrite heart*,” which is an essential part of true repentance (Psalm 51:17). This sorrow was not superficial; he mourned deeply over the sin he had committed and the harm it caused. The depth of his remorse was a sign that he wanted not only forgiveness but a changed heart.

column4: David asked God to “*Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me”* (Psalms 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would prevent him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than just apologizing, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow*” (Psalms 51:7). He recognized that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.
column5: David asked God: “*Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me*” (Psalm 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would keep him from repeating the same mistakes. Instead of merely apologizing, David pleaded with God to purify him, saying: “*Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow*” (Psalm 51:7). He recognized that only God could cleanse his heart and restore his joy.

column4: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways moving forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalms 51:12) demonstrates his hope to be aligned with God in every part of his life.
column5: David’s desire for spiritual renewal reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways thereafter. His request for a “*a willing spirit*” (Psalm 51:12) shows his hope to be in harmony with God in every aspect of his life.

column4: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he was very sick. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).
column5: And although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he became very ill. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to keep the child alive, but when the child died he accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).

column4: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgressions. David’s decision to write down his plea for mercy, creating one of the Bible’s most enduring psalms, shows his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.
column5: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgressions. David’s decision to record his plea for mercy, creating one of the most enduring psalms in the Bible, shows his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony to repentance and restoration for others to learn from, immortalizing his journey from guilt to grace.

column4: David’s repentance journey was not simply about feeling sorry; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart transformation inscribed in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the Bible's most significant examples of genuine repentance.
column5: David’s journey of repentance was not merely a feeling of regret; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through the confession, acceptance, and inner transformation recorded in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the most prominent examples of true repentance in the Bible.
